newsitem.title: USA: Fidelity Magellan manager passes blame for poor returns.
newsitem.headline: Fidelity Magellan manager passes blame for poor returns.

text.p: Fidelity Investments' Magellan Fund manager Bob Stansky, without mentioning his predecessor, Tuesday blamed Jeffrey Vinik's large investments in bonds, cash and cyclical stocks for the giant fund's dismal performance this year.
"That lack of firepower among the fund's largest holdings somewhat limited its returns," Stansky said in a question-and-answer interview published in Magellan's semiannual report.

Since taking the helm of the $53.2 billion fund on June 1 from Vinik, who resigned under widespread criticism to start his own hedge fund, Stansky has slowly shifted the portfolio out of bonds and cash and into stocks.

At the end of September, the most recent date figures are available, Stansky had 88.9 percent of the fund's assets invested in stocks, 9.8 percent in bonds and 1.2 percent in cash, according to Fidelity's monthly fund guide, also released Tuesday.

At the end of May, 19.3 percent of the fund was invested in bonds, 8.5 percent was in cash and other investments, and its top holdings included cyclical shares such as General Motors Corp., Deere & Co. and CSX Corp..

"The bond and cash positions not only had the effect of holding the fund back while the broad stock market rose in 1996, the bond stake negatively impacted performance as investors' fear of higher interest rates drove bond yields higher and prices lower," he said.
Some analysts, however, said Stansky is moving too cautiously to reverse the fund's course.

"I'm just amazed at how slowly he has moved," said David O'Leary, president of Alpha Equity Research, a Portsmouth, N.H.-based firm which tracks Fidelity. "I think they're just too pessimistic about the market."

Despite the changes, Magellan still lags the broad market by a wide margin, returning just 7.00 percent for the first 10 months of the year vs. 16.63 percent for the S&P 500. Lipper Analytical Services ranked Magellan 596th out of 632 growth funds for the one-year period ended Nov. 7.
O'Leary estimates investors have pulled out $3.8 billion from Magellan since the beginning of the year and more than $1 billion in October alone.
In his comments, Stansky struck a note of caution, warning that if the economy slowed, it could hurt stocks.
"If world economies slow, or we begin to see widespread interst rate hikes, the entire U.S. market could be negatively impacted," he said.

Yet, he said the technology sector has many companies with fast-growing earnings. Magellan raised its stake in technology shares to 10.1 percent of assets at the end of September, up from 6.7 percent at the end of August and 2.6 percent when he took over in June.

Stansky said he invested in such technology companies as Intel Corp. and International Business Machines Corp. , both of which showed up in his top 10 holdings list for the first time in September, as well as Cisco Systems Inc. and Oracle Corp..

Several of the fund's top 10 stocks are cyclicals, including GM, Chrysler Corp., CSX and Deere, which have lagged gains in the broad market this year "despite generally favourable business prospects."
"I believe this was tied to investor scepticism that earnings for these companies may have already peaked for this economic cycle," he said.
